# Conjunctivitis - infective: Scenario: Who should I refer to ophthalmology?
## Scenario: Who should I refer to ophthalmology?
### Who should I refer to ophthalmology?
* A [red flag](https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/conjunctivitis-infective/diagnosis/assessment/) indicating a [serious cause](https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/conjunctivitis-infective/diagnosis/differential-diagnosis/) of red eye — have a low threshold for referral to avoid missing sight-threatening conditions.
+ For further information, see the CKS topic on [Red eye](https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/red-eye/) .
* Ophthalmia neonatorum (sticky eye with redness in a neonate).
+ If infection with a sexually transmitted pathogen is confirmed — ensure that the child’s mother and her sexual partners have been referred for appropriate treatment.
* Suspected gonococcal or chlamydial conjunctivitis.
* Consider the possibility of gonorrhoea or chlamydia in sexually active individuals or children of any age in whom sexual abuse is suspected.

## Scenario: Who should I refer to ophthalmology?

From birth onwards.

### Who should I refer to ophthalmology?

**Note: guidance from the College of Optometrists on [urgency of referral](https://www.college-optometrists.org/clinical-guidance/guidance/guidance-annexes/annex-4-urgency-of-referrals-table) includes advice relating to people with different causes of red eye.**

**Arrange urgent assessment by ophthalmology if the person has:**

* A [red flag](https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/conjunctivitis-infective/diagnosis/assessment/) indicating a [serious cause](https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/conjunctivitis-infective/diagnosis/differential-diagnosis/) of red eye — have a low threshold for referral to avoid missing sight-threatening conditions.
  
    + For further information, see the CKS topic on [Red eye](https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/red-eye/) .
* Ophthalmia neonatorum (sticky eye with redness in a neonate).
  
    + If infection with a sexually transmitted pathogen is confirmed — ensure that the child’s mother and her sexual partners have been referred for appropriate treatment.
* Suspected gonococcal or chlamydial conjunctivitis.
* Consider the possibility of gonorrhoea or chlamydia in sexually active individuals or children of any age in whom sexual abuse is suspected. For further information see the CKS topics on [Chlamydia - uncomplicated genital](https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/chlamydia-uncomplicated-genital/) , [Child maltreatment - recognition and management](https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/child-maltreatment-recognition-management/) and [Gonorrhoea](https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/gonorrhoea/) .
* Possible herpes infection.
* Suspected periorbital or orbital cellulitis.
* Severe disease, for example, corneal ulceration, significant keratitis or presence of pseudomembrane.
* Recent intraocular surgery.
* Conjunctivitis associated with a severe systemic condition such as rheumatoid arthritis or immunocompromise.
* Corneal involvement associated with soft contact lens use:
  
    + Do not give antibiotics in the interim as this may interfere with corneal culture.
    + Advise the person to take their contact lenses with them to eye casualty as special diagnostic tests may be required.

**Discuss with/refer to ophthalmology (with urgency dependent on clinical situation) if:**

* There is diagnostic uncertainty or the appropriate diagnostic equipment is not available.
* The person has recurrent or persistent conjunctivitis.
* Conjunctivitis is thought to be due to molluscum contagiosum.

#### Basis for recommendation

The recommendations on when to refer a person to ophthalmology are largely based on expert opinion in the American Academy of Ophthalmology guideline _Conjunctivitis preferred practice pattern_ [ [AAO, 2019](https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/conjunctivitis-infective/references/) ]; the BMJ Best Practice guideline _Acute conjunctivitis_ [ [BMJ Best Practice, 2021](https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/conjunctivitis-infective/references/) ]; the College of Optometrists guidelines _Conjunctivitis (viral, non-herpetic)_ [ [College of Optometrists, 2020](https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/conjunctivitis-infective/references/) ], _Conjunctivitis (bacterial)_ [ [College of Optometrists, 2021b](https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/conjunctivitis-infective/references/) ] _Conjunctivitis, Chlamydial (adult inclusion conjunctivitis)_ [ [College of Optometrists 2021](https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/conjunctivitis-infective/references/) ] and _Ophthalmia neonatorum_ [ [College of Optometrists, 2021a](https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/conjunctivitis-infective/references/) ]; the College of Optometrists _Urgency of referrals table_ [ [College of Optometrists, 2022](https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/conjunctivitis-infective/references/) ]; the Royal College of General Practitioners (RCGP) guideline _Management of infective conjunctivitis in primary care_ [ [RCGP, 2013](https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/conjunctivitis-infective/references/) ]; as well as a number of review articles [ [Azari, 2013](https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/conjunctivitis-infective/references/) ; [Usher, 2014](https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/conjunctivitis-infective/references/) ; [Alfonso, 2015](https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/conjunctivitis-infective/references/) ; [Drew, 2015](https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/conjunctivitis-infective/references/) ].

##### Referral to ophthalmology

* Ophthalmia neonatorum:
  
    + All cases of neonatal sticky eye with redness must be urgently referred to ophthalmology to prevent serious systemic and local complications — management usually involves input from paediatrics [ [RCGP, 2013](https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/conjunctivitis-infective/references/) ; [Drew, 2015](https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/conjunctivitis-infective/references/) ; [AAO, 2019](https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/conjunctivitis-infective/references/) ; [College of Optometrists, 2021a](https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/conjunctivitis-infective/references/) ].
* Herpes infection:
  
    + Systemic herpes simplex infection is a life-threatening condition.
    + Ocular infection with herpes simplex or herpes zoster — requires urgent specialist assessment and treatment with oral antivirals [ [Azari, 2013](https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/conjunctivitis-infective/references/) ; [Alfonso, 2015](https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/conjunctivitis-infective/references/) ; [AAO, 2019](https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/conjunctivitis-infective/references/) ; [College of Optometrists, 2022](https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/conjunctivitis-infective/references/) ].
* Conjunctivitis associated with contact lens use:
  
    + If topical fluorescein reveals corneal staining (epithelial defect) — urgent referral is required as this can be a sight-threatening condition [ [RCGP, 2013](https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/conjunctivitis-infective/references/) ; [Drew, 2015](https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/conjunctivitis-infective/references/) ].
    + Bacterial keratitis can also occur in contact lens wearers [ [Azari, 2013](https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/conjunctivitis-infective/references/) ].
* Recurrent and persistent conjunctivitis — the Royal College of General Practitioners recommends stopping all drops and referring to ophthalmology if symptoms persist after 10 days [ [RCGP, 2013](https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/conjunctivitis-infective/references/) ; [College of Optometrists, 2021b](https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/conjunctivitis-infective/references/) ].
